plate.narration: Tall boundary stones stand across the caravan road. A dragonling grandmother lifts a little bell over a waiting pack. Behind her, wheels and tails crowd the red hills. Everyone wants through. The stones are in no hurry.

objectives.label: Got a prospector to listen to the one rule
Laid out the whole outline of the truth

goal.text: Get past the old boundary stones, and find out why they hold the rush back.

steps.label: Calm the crowd at the stones

facet_unassigned.name: The Unassigned Stone
facet_unassigned.text: Kept by the grandmothers with the list of caves never assigned. Don't you dare sell it.

scene_stones_line.narration: Get past the old boundary stones and find out why they hold the rush back. Tall gray stones lean across the road into the red hills. A crowd waits outside them. Somebody has brought a chair. Somebody else has brought a larger chair.

choices.label: Join the inspection line
Walk straight to the front. You're home.

scene_dragonling_home.narration: A grandmother with glasses on a chain looks up from her tally book, looks at you, and drops the pencil. "Well! Look who came home the FRONT way." Within a minute you have been hugged by four aunts and handed a warm rock to hold. Then her face goes serious. "Worst season in the tallies, love. Come and help."

choices.label: Help at the gate

scene_inspection.narration: A grandmother passes a bell over each pack and tallies every ring. "Rules are rules," she says. "Your turn." She adjusts her glasses, then her pencil, then her glasses again.

choices.label: Open your packs and let her look
Show her you carry no digging tools
Show her Mother Thrum's tuned charm
Risk listing the packs without laying them out

check_not_diggers.prompt: Turn out every pocket and lay your gear in one neat row, fast, so the grandmother can see there is not a pick or a shovel in it

onSuccess.narration: Rope, socks, a squashed sandwich, a spoon. Not one pick, not one shovel, and you never once say the word treasure. The grandmother taps her pencil on her teeth. "Not diggers," she writes. "Very tidy." She waves you through with a look that is almost respect.

onFailure.narration: You lay it all out, but your packs are still ringing like a shop door. The grandmother inspects everything anyway, including your socks, and writes PROBABLY HONEST in the tally book. Then she hugs you, because that is what grandmothers do after an inspection.

scene_inspection_open_packs.narration: The grandmother checks what you actually carry, tallying any humming things. "The tally house will want your account." She sends you through, having inspected the socks twice.

choices.label: Walk on into the gate town

scene_inspection_show_charm.narration: You hold up the witch's charm. Her bell and the charm ring together, the very same note. The grandmother's eyebrows go all the way up. "That's Thrum's work. Is that old crow still sitting at the ford?" She chuckles and waves you straight through. "Anybody Thrum trusts can skip my socks."

choices.label: Walk on into the gate town

scene_gate_town.narration: Bells hang from poles, packs and one goat. Grandmothers check every digging tool. "Take what the mountain drops. Never pry at what it holds," says a grandmother. A man with a huge pry bar says he did not hear. The goat heard.

choices.label: Help the grandmothers act out the rule
Ask what all the bells are for
Say the rule the way your grandmother says it
Risk telling the prospector the rule while he walks away

scene_bell_code.narration: The small bell-code expert explains: one for moths leaving, two for a warm cave, three for come home now. There is an unrung bell too. She stops talking when you ask about that one.

choices.label: Go back and help with the man and his pry bar

scene_gate_town_explain_home.narration: You plant your feet and say it exactly the way your grandmother says it, finger wagging and all: "Take what the mountain drops. Never pry at what it holds. And wipe your feet." The man with the pry bar blinks. Every grandmother in earshot nods so hard their glasses bounce.

choices.label: Watch him think about it

check_one_rule.prompt: Act out the one rule for a stubborn prospector: pick up a fallen pebble nice and easy, then pry at the hill and get flattened

onSuccess.narration: You do not shout the rule at him. You act it out: pick up a pebble the mountain dropped, nice and easy, then pretend to pry at the hill, and pretend the hill sits on you. You fall over flat, very slowly, like a tree. Somewhere in the middle he stops saying "right, right" and starts actually watching.

onFailure.narration: He watches the whole thing, nods along, says "Right, right," and marches off up the hill with his pry bar anyway. You follow him, because somebody should.

scene_rule_heard.narration: The prospector gives up his pry bar. A grandmother hangs it on a wall of hundreds. "Every one of those listened, in the end." She finds a hook between two especially stubborn ones.

choices.label: Walk back past the stones

scene_crab_warning.narration: Up the hill, the prospector is about to pry at a sparkling heap on a patch of warm ground. The heap stands up. It is a glassback crab, and it is doing a slow, clacking dance with its claws raised. Its friend is standing up too.

choices.label: Read the crab's warning dance
Tell everyone exactly what that dance means
Get between the crabs and the prospector
Risk guessing what the crab dance means

check_read_crab.prompt: Read what the glassback crab's dance means

onSuccess.narration: Claws up. Sideways shuffle. Rock to the left. You have seen a cat do something very like it on a warm wall, and you know exactly what the cat meant.

onFailure.narration: You decide the dance means hello. It does not mean hello.

scene_crab_settles.narration: Claws up and a sideways shuffle means: this warm ground is my house. Everybody takes three slow steps back off the warm patch. The crabs stop dancing, settle down, and go back to looking like a very expensive pile of gems. The prospector gives you his pry bar without being asked.

choices.label: Take the pry bar back down the hill

encounter_crabs.narration: The glassback crabs charge, slow and clacking and absolutely sure of themselves.

onVictory.narration: The crabs decide you are more trouble than you are worth and back into their warm burrow, still clacking. The prospector drops his pry bar and runs all the way back down past the stones.

onDefeat.narration: The crabs chase you off their warm patch, down the hill, past the bells, and right back out through the boundary stones.

scene_crabs_rescue.narration: Out past the stones, the grandmothers fish you out of the heather, one collar at a time. They bandage your scrapes, hand everybody a warm rock, and give you a stern look over their glasses. "Bandages cost, this season," says one. "Everything costs, this season." Up the hill, the crabs clack, very pleased with themselves.

choices.label: Pay two coins for the bandages
Give them your supper for the bandages
Work it off on the grandmothers' pry-bar wall

scene_crabs_rescue_pay.narration: You count two coins into a grandmother's palm. She bites each one, writes BANDAGES: PAID in her tally book, and gives everybody a hard candy for being brave. The candy is very good. The coins are gone, and so is the afternoon.

choices.label: Sit down by the stones with the turned-back crowd

scene_crabs_rescue_supper.narration: You hand over your supper. Eleven grandmothers share it out, a crumb each, chew very thoughtfully, and declare it adequate. It was going to be a lovely supper. Your stomachs grumble about it all the way back down to the stones.

choices.label: Sit down by the stones with the turned-back crowd

scene_crabs_rescue_work.narration: The grandmothers keep a wall of pry bars, every one given up by somebody who listened in the end, and a heap more waiting to be hung. You hang them until your arms ache: one hundred and six. By the last one the sun is low, and the afternoon is gone.

choices.label: Sit down by the stones with the turned-back crowd

scene_turned_back.narration: Outside the stones, Wend serves soup under a DEEP HOLLOW flap. Wend knows your names from the north road. A wooden box on the pot reads FOR THE ROOT OF THINGS. A humming crystal hangs beside the ladle.

choices.label: Sit down and eat with the turned-back prospectors
Ask Wend what "the root of things" means
Remind Wend that you said no
Let Wend thank you for your coin

check_ask_wend.prompt: Get a straight answer out of Wend

onSuccess.narration: Wend thinks for a long time. "Everything that hums wants to go home," Wend says at last. "We'd like to help it get there, all at once." It sounds lovely. It also sounds like something nobody should do on a guess. You go up to the tally house thinking about it.

onFailure.narration: Wend answers a different question, beautifully, about the right amount of salt in soup. By the end you know a great deal about salt and nothing at all about roots. Wend waves you off to the tally house with a full bowl.

scene_turned_back_share_soup.narration: You squeeze onto a bench between two prospectors who were turned back at the stones. They grumble about grandmothers, and then they talk about home, and by the second bowl they are talking about going there. Wend listens to everyone and learns everyone's name. The crystal hums along.

choices.label: Go up to the tally house

scene_turned_back_said_no.narration: "We said no," you tell Wend, "on the north road." Wend nods. "I remember. I remember everything about you." Wend fills your bowls anyway, exactly as warmly as before. "Soup's still free. Kindness first." The crystal hums the same note as the stones in your packs.

choices.label: Go up to the tally house

scene_turned_back_coin.narration: Wend greets you like family, hugs everybody, and shows the others your names in the little book. "These ones helped," Wend tells the tent, and everybody claps. It is very warm in the tent. It is warmer than you expected, and you are not entirely sure you like it.

choices.label: Go up to the tally house

scene_tallies.narration: Great-Grandma Ashby opens a book in the tally house. Eruptions fill its pages in orderly marks. This season's page is mostly question marks. "Show me what you know," says Ashby. "We will compare."

choices.label: Hold up Mother Thrum's tuned charm
Sing the spiral verses from the relay
Ask her to read the newest tallies aloud first
Lay out everything you've seen on the floor

scene_tallies_hear_tallies.narration: For a thousand years: moons, small Gemfall, moons again. Ashby reads the old rhythm, then this season's broken one. Somebody has drawn a very worried face in the margin.

choices.label: Now show her what you have brought

scene_charm_rings.narration: The witch's charm rings the moment you hold it up, and Great-Grandma Ashby goes very still. She opens the oldest book on the shelf, the one with the cracked spine, and points to a mark drawn like a little bell. "Same note," she says. "My great-great-grandma heard it too."

choices.label: Lay out the rest of it

scene_verses_sung.narration: You sing the spiral verses, and the grandmothers lay a string on the floor map, landmark by landmark. The roads curl around the gemfalls exactly the way their tally marks do. One grandmother says a word that is not allowed in the tally house.

choices.label: Lay out the rest of it

check_outline.narration: Great-Grandma Ashby sets a piece of chalk in your hand and taps the clues on the floor map, one at a time, in the order that makes the shape. "Watch," she says. "Then put them back the same way. Slowly, dears. The map is older than I am."

interaction.cue: Watch the clues light up, then chalk them back in order.

onSuccess.narration: The one note every stone hums, the songs that curl, the jackalopes going quiet, the tallies breaking: you chalk them all down in the right order, and the shape they make is plain.

onFailure.narration: You get the pieces muddled, so Great-Grandma Ashby moves the chalk marks around with her walking stick, one by one, humming, until the shape is plain.

onAssisted.narration: Great-Grandma Ashby taps the last clue with her walking stick, just once, and the shape on the floor map is plain: the one note every stone hums, the songs that curl, the jackalopes going quiet, the tallies breaking.

scene_here_first.narration: "One more thing," says Great-Grandma Ashby. "The boundary stones were here first. Before the first families. Already marking the line we mark now." She taps the floor map. Everything since Bramblewood points one way: the stones are older than the mountain's name, and the land has always known.

choices.label: Go out and read the oldest stone
Ask what's on the shelf behind her

check_read_stone.prompt: Read the worn marks on the oldest boundary stone

onSuccess.narration: On the oldest stone, under the moss, are rows of marks worn almost smooth. They are tally marks, like the grandmothers' marks, but far older. Somebody was counting here before the first families came. The land has been keeping records. Great-Grandma Ashby only nods. "Now come and see my shelf."

onFailure.narration: The marks are worn so smooth you cannot tell scratches from weather. Great-Grandma Ashby takes your hand and runs your fingers along them: one, one, one, and a gap. "Counting," she says. "Before us. Come and see the shelf."

scene_here_first_onward.narration: Behind Great-Grandma Ashby, on a shelf of its own, something glints. She sees you looking and does not pretend she hasn't. "Clever eyes," she says, and she reaches up with her walking stick, very gently, the way you would touch a sleeping baby's blanket. "Come here, then. Carefully."

choices.label: Step up to the shelf

scene_unassigned.narration: A fresh-fallen gem rests on an old list of caves nobody may gather in. "Keeping," says Great-Grandma Ashby. "Not hiding." Her stick straightens the list without touching the gem.

choices.label: Ask to carry it, as proof for whoever needs to hear
Ask for it the proper way, with a warm rock in both hands
Leave it kept, where it is
Risk lifting the stone before its wrapping is level

scene_unassigned_leave_kept.narration: You leave the stone on its list. Ashby squares the paper with her stick. "Some things want keeping more than carrying." The shelf hums quietly behind you.

choices.label: Step out into the evening

scene_unassigned_ask_proper.narration: You hold the warm rock in both hands and ask, the proper way, the way every dragonling child learns before they learn to fly. Great-Grandma Ashby watches you do it with her mouth pressed tight, and then she lifts the gem off its list and sets it in your hands on top of the rock. "Keeping," she says. "Not taking. You know the difference. Don't you dare sell it."

choices.label: Step out into the evening

check_carry.prompt: Lift the gem off its list the keeping way: two hands, slow as a snail, and set the list straight again after

onSuccess.narration: Two hands, slow as a snail, and you square the list after with one finger. Great-Grandma Ashby wraps the gem in a page torn from nothing important and puts it in your hands. "The Unassigned Stone. Keep it. Don't you dare sell it."

onFailure.narration: Your fingers bump the list crooked, and you grab at the gem as if it might run off. Great-Grandma Ashby pats your hand. "You'll know the difference soon. Not today." The stone stays on its list, and somehow that feels right too.

scene_moths_leaving.narration: Embermoths stream south over the porch. One bell rings. The small bell-code expert tugs your sleeve. "Moths leaving. Every night this month," she says. She knows this code. She wishes she had happier news.

choices.label: Run after the moths and see where they go
Hold out your hands for one to land
Ask why the bells count moths

check_follow_moths.prompt: Everybody run to keep up with a river of embermoths

onSuccess.narration: You run along the hillside under the glowing river. The moths do not drift at random. They flow around every cave where a stone has fallen, the way water flows around a rock, and then carry on south. You come back out of breath, with sparks in your hair.

onFailure.narration: You run, trip over a goat, and lie on your back in the heather watching the moths go over. From down there it is the most beautiful thing you have ever seen. The goat lies down too. Neither of you says anything for a while.

scene_moths_leaving_hold_one.narration: You hold out your hands. One embermoth circles, comes down, and lands, warm as a cup of cocoa. Then it notices your pack. It lifts off at once and flies a wide loop around the humming thing inside before it joins the others going south. The small dragonling pats your arm. "They all do that," she says.

choices.label: Go in to supper

scene_moths_leaving_ask_bells.narration: "Because they always leave a little before the mountain wakes up," says the small dragonling, very fast, "and come back after, and grandmothers count everything." She thinks. "But they've never left this many. And they haven't come back." She rings the moth bell once more, very carefully, as if it might break.

choices.label: Go in to supper

scene_bell_house_supper.narration: Supper in the bell house is a long table, forty grandmothers, and bread baked on hot rocks. Great-Grandma Ashby taps the table with her stick. "Old rule at this table. Every guest brings something. A story, a recipe, a thing from the road." Forty pairs of glasses turn your way, all at once, and wait.

choices.label: Tell them the story of your road
Ask how they bake bread on rocks
Put the Depot Stone on the table, SOLD tag and all
Pay a coin for a pot of honey for the table

check_supper_story.prompt: Tell forty grandmothers a good story

onSuccess.narration: You tell them about the lines and the jackalopes and the roads that bend, and you do all the voices. Forty grandmothers laugh in the right places and gasp in the right places, and one of them cries a little at the end, and says it is the onions.

onFailure.narration: You get the order muddled and tell the end first. The grandmothers do not mind at all. They simply tell it back to you in the right order, interrupting each other, until it is a much better story than the one you started with.

scene_bell_house_supper_ask_recipe.narration: Asking forty grandmothers for one recipe gets you forty recipes, all different, and an argument that lasts until dessert. The only thing they agree on is that you are far too thin. You go to bed carrying a pile of loaves, and a list of instructions you will never fully understand.

choices.label: Go up to bed, very full

scene_bell_house_supper_depot_tag.narration: You set the Depot Stone on the table. The whole bell house goes silent. Great-Grandma Ashby picks up the SOLD tag with two fingers, as if it smells. "Nobody sells what the mountain drops," she says, and she drops the tag in the fire. She pushes the stone back to you. "Now you're keeping it. Not owning it."

choices.label: Go up to bed, thinking

rest_bell_house.narration: Sleep on warm stone under silent bells. A grandmother adds a hot rock to your blanket. Outside, the rush still lines up by lantern light. Inside, even the smallest bell is tucked in.

choices.label: Sleep, until somebody shakes you awake

scene_night_lights.narration: The bell-code expert wakes you. Three lanterns bob toward a hillside cave. "On the list," she whispers. "Nobody gathers there." Her slippers are on the wrong feet. She has not noticed.

choices.label: Wake the grandmothers
Climb up quietly and talk to them
Fly up silently and look first
Have a duskrunner slip up the dark hillside first

check_night_talk.prompt: Talk three night diggers out of a cave

onSuccess.narration: Halfway up you find three young prospectors with lanterns and one shovel. You sit down on a rock with them and tell them about the list, and the one rule, and the grandmothers' bells. They go a bit pale. "We thought it was just a cave," says one. They walk back down with you, and nobody digs.

onFailure.narration: You climb up quietly, step on a bell somebody left in the heather, and it goes CLANG. The three diggers drop everything and run straight back down to the stones. Their shovel stays behind. A grandmother collects it at dawn and hangs it on the wall where the grandmothers keep every pry bar anybody ever gave up.

scene_night_lights_wake_grans.narration: Eleven grandmothers march uphill in nightgowns, ringing hand bells. The lanterns wobble, then flee downhill. Ashby returns yawning. "Thank you, dears. Back to bed."

choices.label: Back to bed

scene_night_lights_fly_look.narration: Your griffin glides up without a sound. The lanterns belong to three young prospectors, not much older than you, with one shovel between them and no idea where they are. You land beside them and point them gently back toward the stones. They go, and say thank you, and do not dig.

choices.label: Glide back to the bell house

scene_morning_bells.narration: "Help the big-bell crew set its supports and learn the passing line," says the bell-code expert, very fast, "or polish the hand bells for a little answering chorus. Either job helps at the morning line!" The corner bell stays untouched, its rope tied high. The bell-code expert keeps looking somewhere else.

choices.label: Pull the biggest bell rope
Help polish the little bells instead
Ask about the bell in the corner
Have a thornguard show everybody how to haul the big rope
Risk hauling the big rope without setting supports

check_big_bell.prompt: Everybody haul on the rope of the biggest bell in the bell house

onSuccess.narration: You haul on the rope. The bell swings, and BONG, the whole hillside hums, and you feel it in your teeth. Far up the hills, other bell houses answer, one after another. The small dragonling says that was very nearly as good as a grandmother.

onFailure.narration: You haul on the rope, and the bell swings, and the rope swings back up and takes you with it. For one glorious moment you are flying. Then the grandmothers catch you, one on each ankle, and the bell rings anyway, louder than ever.

scene_morning_bells_polish.narration: You polish the hand bells until your faces look stretched and silly in them. The expert checks each one, then teaches you where its note fits between the others. She declares the little chorus acceptable. This is her highest mark.

choices.label: Go down to the stones

scene_morning_bells_unrung.narration: You ask about the bell in the corner. The small dragonling, who has talked without stopping since yesterday, stops. "Nobody rings that one," she says quietly. "Not ever. Great-Grandma says we'll know." She reaches up on tiptoe and touches its rim, just once. It is cold, in a house full of warm stones.

choices.label: Go down to the stones

scene_crowd_at_stones.narration: The morning line is pushing. A feathered hat shouts from a cart that the stones are ordinary rocks. The grandmothers hold their ground. "Not one step back, dears," says one grandmother. Help make room, share what you know, or use the bell job you prepared.

choices.label: Climb up and tell the crowd what you have seen
Stand in the line with the grandmothers
Sing the spiral verses, loud
Pass the signal bell down the crew line you practiced
Use the hand-bell chorus you prepared
Risk speaking over the shouting without making room

check_tell_crowd.prompt: Get a shouting crowd to listen

onSuccess.narration: You climb up beside the feathered hat and tell them: the hum, the silent warrens, the roads that bend, the moths going south. You tell it like a story, because it is one. The crowd goes quiet. The feathered hat comes off. Nobody pushes after that.

onFailure.narration: You climb up and start to tell them, and the crowd shouts you down. But while they are shouting at you, nobody is pushing. By the time they run out of breath, the grandmothers have rung for help, and twenty more grandmothers have arrived. The crowd sits down, grumbling.

choice_crowd_at_stones_stand_with.narration: You walk out and stand in the line between two grandmothers, and do not say anything at all. The crowd looks at the old ladies, and at you, and at the old stones. The feathered hat climbs down off his cart, muttering. It is very hard to push past people who are just standing there, being right.

choices.label: Stay until the crowd settles

choice_crowd_at_stones_sing_verses.narration: You sing Old Corran's spiral verses, loud, from the top of a stone. Half the crowd know the old verses and start singing along. Then they reach the new ones, the ones that bend away and away, and their voices trail off. They know those roads. They have walked those bends. The crowd goes very quiet.

choices.label: Let the quiet settle

scene_centaur_whisper.narration: With the crowd settled, centaur guide Perrin Nine-Verse beckons behind a stone. "A Shortcut through the hills. My family has argued about it for nine generations. Nobody has walked it," says Perrin. He checks behind him twice.

choices.label: Walk the Shortcut with him
Thank him and take the caravan road
Show him Old Corran's bark of verses

scene_shortcut.narration: The Shortcut is real. It goes through a crack in a hill, under a rock arch, and comes out at the very last boundary stone, a whole day ahead of the caravan road. Perrin stares at it with tears in his eyes. "Never tell anyone," he says. "Not ever. It's the best argument we've got."

choices.label: Promise never, ever to say so

scene_centaur_whisper_caravan_road.narration: You thank Perrin and choose the caravan road. He looks so relieved that he has to sit down. "Good. Good! The argument lives," he says, wiping his eyes. "My grandfather would have been furious if it ended on a Tuesday." He gallops off to argue about it with someone at once.

choices.label: Go to the last boundary stone

scene_centaur_whisper_show_bark.narration: Perrin reads Old Corran's bark, and his lips move along with the verses. Then he goes pale. "Corran's new verses bend around the falls," he whispers, "and they bend around the Shortcut too. It's in the song. It's been in the song all along." He rolls the bark up and hands it back with shaking hooves. "Don't tell Corran."

choices.label: Go to the last boundary stone

scene_warden_count.narration: At the last stone, Sergeant Holloway has the north-road ledger open. "You again. Good. Counters needed. Picks north: four hundred and twelve. Picks back: nine." The sergeant taps the totals. "I dislike this arithmetic."

choices.label: Help count the picks going through
Ask what the wardens do with all the counting
Swap sky news with the sergeant, flyer to flyer

check_count_picks.prompt: Count every pick in a moving crowd

onSuccess.narration: You count, and count, and your number matches the sergeant's exactly. Holloway writes your names in the ledger under 'Counters, Reliable,' which is apparently a great honor. "The citadel keeps logs," the sergeant says. "Somebody has to."

onFailure.narration: You count four hundred and twelve picks, two goats and a very tall hat. Holloway checks your sums, crosses out the goats, keeps the hat, and writes you down as 'Counters, Enthusiastic.' "Close enough," says the sergeant. "For arithmetic."

scene_warden_count_ask_logs.narration: "We write it down," says Holloway. "Every pick, every ash wind, every moth night. It all goes up to Redspire, and it all goes on a shelf." The sergeant closes the ledger. "Mostly, nobody reads it. Mostly." For a moment, the sergeant looks very tired, and very honest.

choices.label: Walk over to the grandmothers

scene_warden_count_sky_news.narration: Your griffin and the sergeant swap sky news: ash over the peak every evening now, the moths all flying south, and warm wind where there should be cold. Holloway writes all of it down and reads it back twice. "Same as our logs," the sergeant says quietly. "Exactly the same. Thank you."

choices.label: Walk over to the grandmothers

scene_who_to_tell.narration: "Who gets the outline first?" asks Great-Grandma Ashby. "The Skywardens keep logs at their citadel. We grandmothers can send news through the bell towns. Or keep it close until you know more." She taps her stick and waits while you decide.

choices.label: The Skywardens at the citadel. They keep logs.
The gatherers: the grandmothers and the bell towns
Ring your own family's bell, and start the word going
Nobody yet. Keep it close until you're sure.

scene_who_to_tell_ring_home.narration: You ring your own family's bell, the pattern you learned before you could talk. For a moment nothing. Then, from three towns up the hills, faint and clear, a bell rings the pattern back, and then adds the one that means hurry home for supper. Great-Grandma Ashby pretends very hard not to have heard.

choices.label: Walk north through the stones

scene_tell_wardens.narration: A relay runner carries your account to the Skywardens. Ashby sniffs. "They do write things down." She checks that the runner's cord is tied properly.

choices.label: Walk north through the stones

scene_tell_gatherers.narration: The grandmothers ring your news from town to town. Ashby blows her nose very loudly and says it is a cold. Nobody asks why she is smiling.

choices.label: Walk north through the stones

scene_keep_close.narration: You keep the outline in your safest pocket. Ashby nods. "Careful is not the same as quiet. But careful is a start." The bells keep their ordinary morning rhythm.

choices.label: Walk north through the stones

end_through_the_stones.narration: You walk north through the boundary stones into the foothills, with the rush all around you and the bells ringing ordinary rings behind you. Ahead, on a red ridge, stands the dark outline of the Skywardens' citadel. Tonight you camp under the stones that were here first, and they feel, for the first time, like they are on your side.

variants.text: Your morning bell job became a way to give the crowd room.

interaction_pry_bars.narration: You and the prospectors carry the pry bars up to the grandmothers' wall. A grandmother makes room for the enormous one. "Nobody uses that near my stones," she says, hanging it safely out of reach. The last pry bar reaches the wall with a clunk, and the grandmother hangs it up, very pleased. "Wall-hanging rate," she says, and counts three coins into your hands. "Honest work, honestly paid."

choices.label: Continue together

interaction_bell_cart.narration: Before the morning crowd gets any worse, the grandmothers wheel their loudest hand bell down to the stones on a little cart. One wheel has stuck in a rut. "Somebody steer!" calls the small bell-code expert, hopping up and down. "Everybody push! Quickly, quickly, quickly!" she cries.

interaction.cue: Friends push the cart while someone steers it out of the rut.

onSuccess.narration: The wheel pops out of the rut with a CLUNK, and the bell on the cart gives one happy ring all by itself. The small bell-code expert rides the rest of the way down the hill on top of it, bossing the goats.

onFailure.narration: The cart tips, the bell goes BONG upside down, and then a grandmother lifts the whole thing out of the rut with one hand and says nothing at all. It is the most impressive thing you have seen this week.

scene_crawlers_porch.narration: The moment you step out onto the porch, the humming in your packs jumps. Under the boards something clatters. Out scuttle bone crawlers, small and pale and many-legged, the color of old teeth, and they are drawn to the hum like cats to a warm lap. They are heading straight for the tally house door and the rows and rows of books inside, which is the best nest a crawler ever saw. Great-Grandma Ashby plants her walking stick. "Not in my books," she says. "Shoo them off my porch, dears, before they get in the cabinets."

choices.label: Shoo the crawlers off the porch

encounter_crawlers.narration: The crawlers click across the porch boards, straight for the humming packs and the tally house door. Drive them off before they reach the books.

scene_crawlers_shooed.narration: The crawlers click, spin, and scuttle away under the porch in one tidy line, as if they had an appointment. Great-Grandma Ashby counts the books anyway, twice. Then she digs in her apron and hands you a little brass whistle. "One loud note," she says. "Crawlers hate it. So do I. Take it." Above the hills, the first tiny lights are coming out.

choices.label: Look up at the evening sky

scene_crawlers_scattered.narration: The crawlers swarm around and around your boots until the porch is all clatter. Then every grandmother in the tally house comes out ringing a hand bell at once, and the crawlers pop away under the boards like popcorn in reverse. Great-Grandma Ashby wraps everybody in blankets and hands out hot tea. Nobody gets a whistle tonight, but the books are safe. Above the hills, the first tiny lights are coming out.

choices.label: Look up at the evening sky

scene_bell_house_supper_honey.narration: You put a coin on the long table. Forty grandmothers go quiet, and then one of them carries in a pot of honey the size of her head. It goes around the table twice, on bread, on porridge, and once, by mistake, on a glasses case. A grandmother wraps a honeycake in a napkin and slides it into your pack. "For the road," she says. "The coin was a very nice thought."

choices.label: Help tuck the bells in for the night

interaction_bell_tuck.narration: You help Ashby wrap the bells in their soft cloths. One gives a tiny ting, and the grandmothers answer with a soft shhh. Then even the smallest bell is quiet. The last bell goes quiet, and the whole bell house breathes out. A grandmother tucks a bundle of leftover bread into your pack. "Breakfast," she whispers. "Bells sleep better when guests are fed."

choices.label: Continue together

interaction_gear_inventory.narration: Lay out what your hero carries and say what each thing is for. The grandmother checks beside you. One sock has been mistaken for a digging tool. It is a particularly stiff sock.

choices.label: Show what I carry
Explain what my gear is for
Ask her to check with me

interaction_one_rule.narration: Show the one rule together: take what the mountain drops; never pry at what it holds. Each hero adds a small part. The grandmother plays the mountain. She is excellent at standing firmly in one place.

interaction.cue: Each hero acts a part of the one rule.

options.label: Pretend to pick up a fallen pebble
options.reaction: You pick up what fell freely. The grandmother mountain nods.

options.label: Show why the pry bar must stop
options.reaction: You stop the pretend pry bar before it touches the grandmother mountain.

options.label: Be the mountain holding something safe
options.reaction: You hold your hands closed. The prospector finally watches what the rule means.

onSuccess.narration: The prospector watches the whole little play. He lowers his pry bar and asks the grandmother where to leave it.

onFailure.narration: He watches the whole thing, nods along, says "Right, right," and marches off up the hill with his pry bar anyway. You follow him, because somebody should.

onAssisted.narration: The grandmother adds the missing part beside you. Together you show the rule, and the prospector lowers his bar.

interaction_crab_warning.narration: Watch the crab's warning: claws up, shuffle sideways, then leave its warm patch. Echo that order to show the prospector how to back away. Nobody needs to be pinched for the lesson.

interaction.cue: Watch the warning, then echo the safe response in order.

onSuccess.narration: You echo the warning and guide everyone back off the warm patch.

onFailure.narration: You decide the dance means hello. It does not mean hello.

onAssisted.narration: The prospector copies your first two steps. Together you check the last one and back off the warm ground.

interaction_kept_stone.narration: Great-Grandma Ashby agrees to let you carry the stone if you can keep its wrapping level. Raise or lower your side, then lift it gently. Her walking stick hovers over the list, ready to straighten it.

interaction.cue: Level the wrapped stone before lifting it from the list.
interaction.objectLabel: The Unassigned Stone in its wrapping

onSuccess.narration: You level the wrapped stone before lifting it. Great-Grandma Ashby checks the list, then gives permission to carry the Unassigned Stone north.

onFailure.narration: Your fingers bump the list crooked, and you grab at the gem as if it might run off. Great-Grandma Ashby pats your hand. "You'll know the difference soon. Not today." The stone stays on its list, and somehow that feels right too.

onAssisted.narration: Great-Grandma Ashby supports the wrapping with her stick. With that help, you lift the stone, and she gives permission to carry it north.

interaction_dawn_rope.narration: Brace the big bell's rope while the acting hero guides the dawn pull. Alone, use the fixed cleat. The expert teaches the crew's hand-to-hand line for bringing help to the line. She has a clipboard almost as tall as she is.

interaction.cue: Hold the rope supports while the acting hero guides the dawn pull.

onSuccess.narration: The dawn bell rings cleanly. You practice the crew's passing line for the line.

onFailure.narration: You haul on the rope, and the bell swings, and the rope swings back up and takes you with it. For one glorious moment you are flying. Then the grandmothers catch you, one on each ankle, and the bell rings anyway, louder than ever.

onAssisted.narration: A grandmother sets the cleat beside you. Together you ring the dawn bell and practice the crew line.

interaction_crowd_bell_line.narration: Use the crew line you practiced. Pass a small signal bell down to the grandmothers at the crowded gate. They can call the next row forward without anybody pushing. Keep it hand to hand, not over the feathered hat.

interaction.cue: Catch the signal bell and pass it toward the gate.

onSuccess.narration: The bell reaches the gate. The grandmothers call the line forward in rows until the pushing stops.

onFailure.narration: A grandmother catches the bell before it drops. She leads the line into rows while you help keep the gap clear.

onAssisted.narration: A grandmother fills the gap in the line beside you. Together you deliver the bell and settle the line.

interaction_crowd_hand_bells.narration: Fit your polished bells between the grandmothers' notes. Each hero adds a turn. The expert points to the next row, and people begin listening for their place. The feathered hat has to stop shouting to hear his row called.

interaction.cue: Each hero adds a hand-bell answer to the prepared chorus.

options.label: Answer after the low bell
options.reaction: Your answer follows the low bell. The next row waits for its turn.

options.label: Answer after the high bell
options.reaction: Your answer follows the high bell. The expert waves one row forward.

options.label: Leave a space for the next answer
options.reaction: You leave a clear space. The waiting crowd hears the next little bell.

onSuccess.narration: The prepared chorus gives each row its turn. The crowd settles, with room around the stones.

onFailure.narration: The expert fills the missing note. The line settles while you keep the space clear.

onAssisted.narration: The expert guides the answers beside you. Together you settle the line with the hand bells.

interaction_crowd_account.narration: The grandmothers make a place beside the cart for your account. Each hero shares something witnessed here, or asks for one of the tallies to be read. You do not have to outshout the feathered hat. The hat is running out of breath.

choices.label: Describe the moths we saw leaving
Ask Ashby to read the changed tallies
Explain the boundary rule in my own words

interaction_gear_inventory_response_show.narration: The grandmother checks the things you show against her tally. The grandmother finishes checking the packs. She records your actual gear and waves you through.

choices.label: Continue together

interaction_gear_inventory_response_use.narration: She writes the uses beside the gear. The sock receives a question mark. The grandmother finishes checking the packs. She records your actual gear and waves you through.

choices.label: Continue together

interaction_gear_inventory_response_chec.narration: She helps check one pocket at a time, leaving room for your answer. The grandmother helps name the gear, then records what you showed. The inspection is complete.

choices.label: Continue together

interaction_crowd_account_response_moths.narration: Your account of the southbound moths gives the waiting people something to listen to. The grandmothers repeat your account down the line. The crowd listens, and the pushing stops.

choices.label: Continue together

interaction_crowd_account_response_talli.narration: Ashby reads the broken pattern aloud. The feathered hat stops to hear the numbers. The grandmothers repeat your account down the line. The crowd listens, and the pushing stops.

choices.label: Continue together

interaction_crowd_account_response_rule.narration: You explain what is freely dropped and what must stay held. A listener lowers a digging tool. The grandmothers repeat your account down the line. The crowd listens, and the pushing stops.

choices.label: Continue together

voiceGuide.tone: warm, loud dragonling home country under a worried sky; grandmothers in charge, bells everywhere, a little spooky about the unrung bell, never scary

npcVoices.great_gran_ashby: the oldest dragonling grandmother; brisk, tender, unarguable, taps things with her walking stick
npcVoices.grandmother: a gate-town grandmother; glasses on a chain, counts everything, hugs first and inspects later
npcVoices.small_dragonling: a bell-code expert aged about six; talks at top speed until the unrung bell comes up
npcVoices.prospector: a stubborn rush prospector with a pry bar; says 'right, right' and doesn't listen until he does
npcVoices.perrin: Perrin Nine-Verse, a centaur guide; conspiratorial, emotional, desperate the Shortcut stays an argument
npcVoices.wend: a Deep Hollow ladler from the north road; gentle, generous, remembers every name, certain the world can be fixed at the root
npcVoices.sergeant_holloway: a Skywarden supply sergeant from the north road; rigid, honest, calls everything 'arithmetic', writes everything down
npcVoices.feathered_hat: a loud prospector on a cart; blustering, sure the stones are just old rocks, quiet once he really listens

interaction_pry_bars.narration: Prospectors hand over pry bars at the stones. Pass them up the slope to the grandmothers' wall. A grandmother has left room for the huge one. She is an optimist.

interaction.cue: Catch the pry bar, then pass it up the line.

onSuccess.narration: The last pry bar reaches the wall with a clunk, and the grandmother hangs it up, very pleased. "Wall-hanging rate," she says, and counts three coins into your hands. "Honest work, honestly paid."

onFailure.narration: One pry bar slips, and a prospector catches it with his boot. "Ow," he says, bravely. The line laughs, and the pry bars go on up the hill.

onAssisted.narration: The grandmother takes the heavy end herself, and together you pass the pry bars up the slope without a single clunk. She counts three coins into your hands. "Wall-hanging rate," she says.

interaction_bell_tuck.narration: Help tuck the bells in with soft cloths so they will not ring in the night. "Company helps," says Ashby. A little bell gives a sleepy ting before you reach it.

interaction.cue: Tuck the bells in for the night, any way you like.

options.label: Drape a cloth over a bell
options.reaction: The bell settles with a very small, sleepy tink.

options.label: Hum a bell lullaby
options.reaction: Every bell on the rafters hums along, softly.

options.label: Give one a last polish
options.reaction: The bell shines, and you can see your sleepy face in it.

stages: Most of the bells are tucked in.
The whole bell house is hushed.

onSuccess.narration: The last bell goes quiet, and the whole bell house breathes out. A grandmother tucks a bundle of leftover bread into your pack. "Breakfast," she whispers. "Bells sleep better when guests are fed."

onFailure.narration: One small bell goes ting at the very last second. Forty grandmothers say shhh at once, and then they all giggle, and the bell house settles down for the night anyway.

interaction_gear_inventory.narration: Lay out what your hero carries and say what each thing is for. The grandmother checks beside you. One sock has been mistaken for a digging tool. It is a particularly stiff sock.

interaction.cue: Each hero names a real item and explains its use.

options.label: Show what I carry
options.reaction: The grandmother checks the things you show against her tally.

options.label: Explain what my gear is for
options.reaction: She writes the uses beside the gear. The sock receives a question mark.

options.label: Ask her to check with me
options.reaction: She helps check one pocket at a time, leaving room for your answer.

onSuccess.narration: The grandmother finishes checking the packs. She records your actual gear and waves you through.

onFailure.narration: You lay it all out, but your packs are still ringing like a shop door. The grandmother inspects everything anyway, including your socks, and writes PROBABLY HONEST in the tally book. Then she hugs you, because that is what grandmothers do after an inspection.

onAssisted.narration: The grandmother helps name the gear, then records what you showed. The inspection is complete.

interaction_crowd_account.narration: The grandmothers make a place beside the cart for your account. Each hero shares something witnessed here, or asks for one of the tallies to be read. You do not have to outshout the feathered hat. The hat is running out of breath.

interaction.cue: Each hero shares evidence or asks for a tally to be read.

options.label: Describe the moths we saw leaving
options.reaction: Your account of the southbound moths gives the waiting people something to listen to.

options.label: Ask Ashby to read the changed tallies
options.reaction: Ashby reads the broken pattern aloud. The feathered hat stops to hear the numbers.

options.label: Explain the boundary rule in my own words
options.reaction: You explain what is freely dropped and what must stay held. A listener lowers a digging tool.

onSuccess.narration: The grandmothers repeat your account down the line. The crowd listens, and the pushing stops.

onFailure.narration: You climb up and start to tell them, and the crowd shouts you down. But while they are shouting at you, nobody is pushing. By the time they run out of breath, the grandmothers have rung for help, and twenty more grandmothers have arrived. The crowd sits down, grumbling.

onAssisted.narration: Ashby helps read the evidence beside you. Together you give the crowd an account it can hear.
